planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer; transplant outdoors only after frost danger has fully passed, as young plants are tender.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this evergreen Cretan subshrub is extremely drought tolerant once established and resents winter wet far more than cold. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a compact, bushy habit and remove any frost-damaged tips in spring. The species is named for the gall-induced, apple-like swellings ('sage apples') that form on stems where a gall wasp lays eggs; these galls have been traditionally candied and eaten in Crete. Leaves can be harvested for a strong, camphorous culinary or tea use similar to common sage.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in a well-draining mix; transplant after frost danger passes, since young growth is more cold-sensitive than mature, woody-based plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; this southeastern European and Anatolian shrubby sage tolerates heat and drought well but needs sharp drainage to survive winter. Cut back hard in early spring to remove winter dieback and encourage dense, bushy new growth from the woody base. Leaves are densely white-woolly and highly aromatic, and are gathered in Turkey and the Balkans as a common 'sage tea' (adacayi) alongside Salvia fruticosa. Avoid overhead watering, as the felted foliage is prone to rot in humid, wet conditions.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow in a prepared bed once soil is workable; plants form a large felted rosette the first year and typically flower and set seed the second year before declining.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage over winter matters more than cold protection, as this Mediterranean biennial/short-lived perennial is grown chiefly for its huge, dramatic, silver-white woolly basal rosette. Remove any wet, rotting lower leaves promptly and keep the crown free of mulch piling against it. In the second year it sends up branched spikes of small whitish-pink flowers; deadhead or allow to self-sow, since plants typically die after flowering (monocarpic). Protect young rosettes from slug damage and excess winter moisture, the two most common causes of loss.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable, or in autumn where winters are mild; seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate well and establishes readily in poor, dry soils.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this low, rosette-forming Eurasian sage thrives in dry banks, grassy verges, and poor lawns where richer soil would cause it to flop or rot. Mow or shear after the pale blue-lilac flower spikes fade to tidy the rosette and curb self-seeding, as plants spread readily by seed in favorable sites. Historically the mucilaginous seeds were moistened and used to soothe irritated eyes, giving rise to the common name 'clary' (from 'clear eye'). It needs minimal watering once established and makes a useful low-care filler for dry gravel gardens and meadow plantings.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost or divide established clumps in spring; transplant after frost danger passes, as new growth is more cold-tender than the established crown.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this vigorous, large-leaved Sardinian sage forms a robust clump of broad, felted, eucalyptus-scented foliage topped by spikes of pale blue-and-white flowers in summer. Cut the clump back hard after flowering or in early spring to refresh foliage and maintain a tidy habit. Leaves are traditionally used in Sardinia to flavor vermouth, amaro, and other herbal liqueurs, and can be dried for aromatic culinary use in the same way as common sage. Established plants are drought tolerant but benefit from occasional deep watering during prolonged summer heat to keep leaves from scorching.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost in a gritty, fast-draining mix; transplant after frost danger passes into a scree bed or raised rock garden with sharp drainage.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this low, mat-forming sage from the mountains of Iran, Turkey, and the Caucasus is a classic rock-garden and scree plant that resents heavy, wet, or richly fertile soil. Shear lightly after the small lilac-purple flower spikes fade to keep the mound tight and promote dense new growth. The crinkled, strongly aromatic gray-green leaves have long been gathered locally for tea and as a seasoning herb, similar in use to common sage but milder. It is highly drought tolerant once established and is best sited where winter moisture drains away quickly from the crown.
